body.heading: Twelve grapes at midnight
paragraphs: In Spain, the last twelve seconds of the year come with a challenge: eat one grape with each of the twelve chimes of the clock at midnight, and the year ahead is said to be lucky. It is harder, and funnier, than it sounds, and whole families practise their grape technique in the days before.

Elsewhere the luck is worn: in the Philippines, round shapes symbolise coins and prosperity, so polka dots are worn and round fruits displayed at New Year. In Brazil, many people wear white for peace and head to the beach, where offerings of flowers are made to the sea.

body.heading: First steps and fresh starts
paragraphs: Scotland's Hogmanay has first-footing: the first person to cross your threshold after midnight brings luck, traditionally arriving with gifts like coal, salt, or whisky — symbols of warmth, flavour, and good cheer for the year. Denmark greets the year by standing on chairs and leaping into it, literally, at midnight.

Underneath the variety is a shared recipe: mark the turning, carry something symbolic across it, and do it together. Noise, too, is nearly universal — bells, pots, fireworks — originally meant to scare off the old year's spirits, now mostly joy with a historical excuse.

body.heading: Start one of your own
paragraphs: A family can borrow the recipe without borrowing a culture wholesale: one symbolic act, done together, at the turning of the year. A candle lit, a door opened to let the old year out, a wish written and kept in a jar to be read next December.
Children take to invented customs instantly and enforce them with the full weight of tradition by the second year. Choose yours carefully; you will be doing it for decades.
